reasons: Seven images in three visual sets: A, B and C are pixel-identical (smooth shading, no grid); D and E are pixel-identical (voxel grid lines, unlabelled two-view sheet); F and G are pixel-identical (voxel grid lines, labelled 'Front, from south-east' and 'Back, from north-west'). F and G tie for first. Their labels show the entrance side, and the back view shows the windows on the far wall, so the build can be checked from both sides. The grid lines show each block, which makes the stepped spruce roof, the 16-block height and the stone walls easy to count against the brief. D is third: same geometry as F and G, but with no labels to tell the viewer which face is the front. A, B and C are the cleanest and most polished in shading, but their smooth surfaces hide the block structure, so the brief's cell-level details (chiseled band, moss base, quoins) are harder to verify; they rank below D. On accuracy, all seven share the same geometry: a squat 10 x 10 stone box with a wide spruce roof. It reads more as a stone hut with a big roof than as a tall watchtower, so none gets full marks there. The visible items match the brief: stone walls, four windows, the door on the south face, the path, the two standing lanterns, the red poppies and the grass yard.
